column4: In the oath-expiration rule, this ayah requires feeding ten poor people from the average food one gives one’s own household. That is a concrete household-to-poor transfer matching the section’s filled bowl and food for the miskin.

The section’s al-maʿūn list names useful everyday household things; 2:267 warns against selecting for charity what the giver would accept only with eyes closed, a specific standard for the quality of goods shared.

The brothers find their traded goods returned in their baggage and say they can now obtain provisions for their family. This is not a borrowed pot, but it is a specific, indirect parallel to the section’s claim that small goods given from a household often return while the household gets what it needs.

After the provisions and hidden cup of 12:70, the brothers turn back and ask what is missing; 12:72 names the king’s cup. The section’s inventory of loanable household objects has a concrete, though royal and accusatory, counterpart in this missing vessel.

The section depicts a householder withholding small material benefits; 16:71 asks why those favored in provision would not share their provision with those under their authority, making withheld household resources a concrete analogy in its argument against denying God’s favor.

This ayah repeats the provision-sharing comparison in 16:71 as a question about whether people would accept those under their authority as equal partners in their provision; it sharpens the section’s closed-hand image into a question of who is allowed a share.

The ayah allocates a share of war gains to orphans, the needy, and the traveler; it gives a concrete instance of household-like resources being directed to the very vulnerable recipients whom the section’s man leaves without support.

The ayah assigns communal wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so it will not circulate only among the rich; this directly counters the section’s image of useful provisions kept within one household.

The section defines the orphan as a child left fatherless and makes the home’s provisions part of that child’s vulnerability; 4:9 asks people handling inheritance to imagine leaving weak offspring behind and fear for them, between 4:8’s instruction to give and 4:10’s warning against consuming orphan property.

This ayah addresses orphan girls whose guardians withhold what is due to them and commands justice toward vulnerable children; it extends the section’s fatherless-child scene from food and shelter to the guardian’s duty not to deny her rights.

The disciples ask Jesus for a table spread with food from heaven; the section names the sofra cloth among ordinary household goods and develops food placed in a filled bowl, so this is a direct table-and-meal scene.
This ayah says the disciples want to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured; it completes the request in 5:112 by stating the meal’s role for those who will share it.
Jesus asks for a table to be sent down as a feast for the first and last of them; this ayah supplies the communal meal requested in 5:112 and connects a shared table with provision.

God answers that the table will be sent down and sets a severe boundary for anyone who disbelieves afterward; it completes 5:112–114’s scene of provision with the consequence attached to receiving it.

The section’s cited household-benefit list includes a knife among ordinary items that may be borrowed; 12:31 places knives in the women’s hands during a gathering at the house, a specific domestic-use scene for one of those small tools.

The section identifies a withholding man as stingy and tight-fisted; 92:8 describes one who is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient, giving a specific account of the attitude behind keeping small household benefits back.

After the stingy person of 92:8, this ayah says he denies the best; it adds the refusal that leads into the consequence in 92:10, matching the section’s act of withholding rather than merely its household setting.

This ayah allows a feeding ransom for a poor person in the context of fasting; it is a concrete measured food provision for a miskin, matching the section’s link between food and the person left without it.

For a hunting violation during pilgrimage, this ayah allows an expiation by feeding needy people; the specific food-for-needy provision offers another concrete instance of the transfer the section’s withholding scene suppresses.
This ayah requires feeding sixty poor people when the prescribed fast cannot be performed; the measured number and meal make the section’s food for the miskin a specific act of provision.

The section defines the orphan as a child whose father has died and places household food under that child’s care; 2:233 assigns the nursing mother’s food and clothing to the father, showing the household support whose loss makes the orphan vulnerable.
